steps.premise: unspecified
steps.action: Use a thin white sheet for the screen.
steps.consequence: People in front can see the shadows through the material.
steps.quote: A thin white sheet lets the shadows show through to the audience.

steps.premise: Folds in the screen can distort the silhouettes.
steps.action: Stretch the sheet tightly over its frame.
steps.consequence: The shadow shapes stay clear.
steps.quote: Pull it taut across the frame so folds don't break up the shapes.

steps.premise: Thin puppet necks buckle when children wave the puppets.
steps.action: Reinforce each slender neck with a second strip of card glued behind it.
steps.consequence: The puppet stays intact through the performance.
steps.quote: Puppets with slender necks tend to fold when children wave them. Glue a second strip of card behind each neck so the figures last through the show.

steps.premise: Children will be handling figures near the light during the show.
steps.action: Before families arrive, test a cool-running LED for a single clear shadow.
steps.consequence: Children can work near the lamp and the audience can follow each outline.
steps.quote: Try the lamp before the families arrive. A cool-running LED that casts one clean shadow lets children handle the figures nearby and keeps the outlines easy to follow.

steps.premise: Some children have trouble gripping a thin puppet stick.
steps.action: Provide large loop handles for those children.
steps.consequence: They can operate their character themselves.
steps.quote: Make a few large loop handles for children who find a narrow stick difficult to hold. They can move their own characters without an adult taking over.

steps.premise: A child may arrive halfway through the session.
steps.action: Set prepared figures beside the uncut card.
steps.consequence: Latecomers can take part in a scene before playtime ends.
steps.quote: Offer some ready-cut figures beside the blank card. A child who arrives halfway through can join a scene while there is still time to play.

steps.premise: Head-on puppets can cast a featureless oval shadow.
steps.action: Cut the figures in side view.
steps.consequence: The audience can identify a character's nose or beak.
steps.quote: A puppet facing straight ahead may look like a plain oval on the sheet. Cut it in profile so the audience can recognize its nose or beak.

steps.premise: The distance between a puppet and the lamp changes its shadow size.
steps.action: Let children experiment by moving one puppet closer to and farther from the lamp.
steps.consequence: They learn how to make a small character appear giant.
steps.quote: Let children try moving the same puppet toward and away from the lamp. Seeing its shadow grow and shrink gives them a way to turn a small character into a giant.

steps.premise: Waiting children can accidentally cast shadows onto the screen.
steps.action: Mark the edge of the performance space with bright tape.
steps.consequence: Children waiting their turn can stay behind the line and out of the picture.
steps.quote: Mark where the performing space ends with a strip of bright tape. Children waiting for a turn can stay behind the line without casting an unexpected head on the screen.

steps.premise: A child may prefer to take part offstage.
steps.action: Let the child shake a sealed jar of rice to imitate rain.
steps.consequence: The scene gets a rain sound and the child has a role.
steps.quote: A child who would rather stay offstage can supply rain by shaking rice in a sealed jar. The scene gains a sound effect and the child gets a part.

steps.premise: Adult shoulders can block the youngest spectators' view.
steps.action: Seat young children on cushions at the front.
steps.consequence: They can see the entire screen.
steps.quote: Give the youngest audience members cushions on the floor at the front. They can see the whole screen without having to look around adult shoulders.

steps.premise: Young performers may forget the order of a scene and may not read.
steps.action: Display a short sequence of pictures behind the screen.
steps.consequence: Performers can see what happens next.
steps.quote: Pin up a short picture sequence behind the screen. Young performers who lose their place can spot what comes next without needing to read.

steps.premise: A solo narrator can otherwise speak every line.
steps.action: Give the audience a repeated line to say on the appearance of the moon.
steps.consequence: Everyone gets to speak in the show.
steps.quote: A single narrator can end up doing all the talking. Give the audience a refrain to call out when the moon appears so everyone gets a line.

steps.premise: An abrupt change to darkness bothers some children.
steps.action: Warn children before the show starts and lower the lights gradually.
steps.consequence: Children have time to settle in.
steps.quote: Some children dislike a room going dark all at once. Dim the lights in stages and tell them when the show is about to start so they can settle in.

steps.premise: A wheelchair user and a standing child may perform together.
steps.action: Keep one side of the screen reachable at seated height with an open approach.
steps.consequence: The seated child can bring a figure into the same scene as their partner.
steps.quote: Leave a clear approach to one side of the screen at seated height. A child using a wheelchair can bring a puppet into the same scene as a standing partner.

steps.premise: Holes must be punched in the figures for their joints.
steps.action: Place scrap card beneath each figure before punching.
steps.consequence: The holes have clean edges and the tables avoid dents.
steps.quote: Put a piece of scrap card under each figure when punching holes for joints. The hole comes out clean and the hall tables stay free of dents.

steps.premise: Children operating figures from behind the sheet miss the audience's perspective.
steps.action: Have partners switch positions after each short scene.
steps.consequence: Both can see how their puppetry looks from the front.
steps.quote: Children behind the sheet can't see the faces out front. Let pairs trade places after each short scene so they can see how their work looks from the audience.

steps.premise: Sticks in a heap can tangle when a performer reaches for a figure.
steps.action: Place each scene's figures in their own shallow tray.
steps.consequence: Performers can find the needed puppet without separating tangled sticks.
steps.quote: Keep figures for each scene in a separate shallow tray. A performer reaching for the dragon can find it without untangling a heap of sticks.

steps.premise: Children already know the characters in a familiar story.
steps.action: Have each child invent a different ending for that story.
steps.consequence: They have more time to perform their new ending.
steps.quote: Invite each child to make up a different ending for a familiar tale. Knowing the characters already leaves more time to act out the new idea.

steps.premise: Children want to demonstrate their puppets after returning home.
steps.action: Pack each finished figure in a paper sleeve for the journey.
steps.consequence: The limbs reach home intact.
steps.quote: Children often want to show someone at home how their puppets work. Send each figure home in a paper sleeve so its limbs survive the trip.

steps.premise: Children need to see which colors will show on the screen.
steps.action: Set colored translucent paper samples next to the silhouettes for children to test against the light.
steps.consequence: They can select a color visible in projection.
steps.quote: Set out a small sample of colored translucent paper beside the silhouettes. Children can hold it up to the light and choose a color that actually shows on the screen.
